reason: The sources provide 18 well-supported claims from distinct sites, detailing the 1959 far side photos, the mechanics of tidal bulges, and other tidally locked bodies in the universe.
story: Think the Moon doesn't spin? That's a myth. The Moon actually rotates on its axis, but it does so at the exact same speed it orbits Earth. This cosmic synchronization, called synchronous tidal locking, keeps the same side facing us forever. In fact, humanity didn't catch a single glimpse of the Moon's far side until 1959, when the Soviet spacecraft Luna 3 transmitted the first photographs. This locking isn't a coincidence; it is driven by gravity. Earth's gravity stretches the Moon, creating tidal bulges. As the Moon spins, these bulges get carried out of alignment, generating gravitational torque that slows its rotation. The lost rotational energy is released as heat, and to conserve momentum, the Moon slowly drifts away from Earth by 1.5 inches (4 cm) each year. Eventually, even Earth would lock to the Moon, but the Sun will likely engulf both first!
angle: The Moon actually spins on its axis, but it matches its orbital speed so perfectly that its far side was completely hidden from humanity until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959.

claims.claim: The Moon rotates around its own axis.
The Moon's rotation period is equal to its orbital period around Earth.
Because the Moon's rotation is synchronized with its orbit, the same side of the Moon always faces Earth.
Humanity did not see the far side of the Moon until 1959.
The Soviet spacecraft Luna 3 captured and transmitted the first photographs of the Moon's far side.
All nineteen known Solar System moons that are large enough to be round are tidally locked to their planets.
Tidal locking is caused by gravitational forces stretching co-orbiting bodies into elongated shapes or bulges.
Because the body rotates, these tidal bulges are carried out of alignment with the line pointing directly toward the partner body.
Gravity pulls on the misaligned bulges, creating torque that slows down the body's rotation.
The energy from continuous tidal stretching of the body is dissipated in the form of heat.
As the Moon's rotation slowed, its orbit expanded, causing it to drift further away from Earth to conserve angular momentum.
The Moon is currently drifting away from Earth at a rate of approximately 4 centimeters (1.5 inches) per year.
The Moon's tidal forces are also gradually slowing down the Earth's own rotation.
Earth's day length increases by about 2 to 2.3 milliseconds per century due to tidal forces.
Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, are mutually tidally locked to each other.
Earth observers can actually see up to 59 percent of the Moon's total surface over time due to libration.
Close binary stars can be tidally locked to one another.
The star Tau Boötis is tidally locked to its extremely close giant planet Tau Boötis b.

disputed: The exact slowing rate of Earth's rotation (S1 states 2.3 milliseconds per century, while S4 states 2 milliseconds; a script should use 'about 2 milliseconds').

Whether Earth will ever tidally lock to the Moon (S1 states it is not expected before the Sun becomes a red giant and engulfs them, while S2 and S6 discuss it as a theoretical eventuality in 50 billion years if they survive the Sun's red giant phase; a script should frame this as a theoretical possibility cut short by the Sun's death).
